doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

chapter: Johnny Hammond, Dreams and moving to New York
title: Danny Wright's band and joining Johnny Hammond in Boston
summary: Recommended by Danny Wright, he played seven nights a week with Johnny Hammond at the Big M while still at school.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Okay. It got to a point at Berklee where, did you feel like I’m ready to get out and play? Well let me rephrase that. Did you get out and play, like with Johnny Hammond, before you felt you were ready?

I think I was — I was nervous about it and I was still in school when I was playing with Johnny Hammond. I mean I might have been in my third year, I mean, and I got recommended to Johnny Hammond through — I used to play in a rhythm & blues band called the Danny Wright Orchestra. And Danny Wright’s band had an interesting rhythm section. It actually had a drummer that became my drummer years later, Peter Donald, who lives in California, a wonderful pianist named Carl Schroeder, who is a mad scientist who teaches out in California at one of the music institutes. But it was like three or four horns and a rhythm section. And I started to play a lot in this band, also Mark Levine, the trombone player who you may be familiar with, he plays trombone and piano, and got a lot of help playing in that band, I learned a lot and then Danny thought I was, the leader though well you could play with this guy Johnny Hammond, he’s looking for a guitar player, I’ll recommend you. I said, “Really, you think, I mean, you think I could do this?” He said, “Well you know a lot of standards, right?” I said I knew a fair amount. And that was it. He just called up Johnny and Johnny said well bring your guitar down to this club, and it was a club in Boston which is no longer in existence. But it was near a club that still functions as a club now called Wally’s that a lot of the students go to. And Wally’s was there when I was a kid but this other club was called the Big M, which stood for Morley’s on the Avenue. I never met Mr. Morley, I don’t think I ever wanted to meet Mr.

Morley, you know. It wasn’t important. But that’s where we played seven nights a week and a matinee on Sunday. And you’d play like three or four sets a night. You know you’d play ‘till like two in the morning, and you’d get up and go to school. And it was at that point where I realized I really wanted to be a player. I was out playing professionally then, and playing with people that had nothing to do with the school, a guy that wouldn’t know one mode from the other, could care less how much you knew. All he just really wanted to know, did you know the song? Could you swing? Could you play the right changes? Could you play four-four rhythm like Freddie Green? He said “play four-four, man, I just want to hear four-four.” Or Charleston. Really simple, but then once he got to know you you could play almost anything. It was a real great place to learn to become more of a traditional musician and also, a thing that doesn’t exist anymore, these kind of apprenticeships in places, especially for a guitarist, especially now that all the organ players are dying. I mean Jack McDuff’s gone, Groove Holmes is gone, Johnny’s gone. And those were the places where young guitar players got a lot of that experience. And it doesn’t happen anymore. So I was lucky that I got in when I did and, yeah, it was at that point that I kind of knew I wanted to play. I still wasn’t totally secure in what was going on but I knew I wanted to play that kind of music. And then everything changed, then it became the late 60s and I met Michael and Randy Brecker and they recommended me for a band called Dreams, which was a fusion band with a singer. So I went to New York and started playing.
